reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Neurocutaneous Disorders (current reference texts)
clinicalPearls: Characterised by unilateral arteriovenous malformations affecting the retina, optic pathway and midbrain, typically along a single embryonic axis
It is a sporadic, non-hereditary condition regarded as a somatic mosaic vascular malformation syndrome
Cutaneous vascular naevi may occur on the same side of the face, overlying the deeper malformations
The retinal arteriovenous malformation appears as dilated, tortuous vessels (racemose angioma) and can threaten vision
Intracranial arteriovenous malformations may present with headache, seizures, haemorrhage or neurological deficit
The size of the retinal lesion broadly correlates with the likelihood of intracranial involvement, so ocular findings prompt neuroimaging
Management is generic and specialist-led: neurosurgical or endovascular assessment of intracranial lesions and ophthalmological monitoring of the retinal malformation
reference.pathophysiology: Wyburn-Mason syndrome is a sporadic vascular malformation disorder thought to arise from a post-zygotic somatic event affecting mesodermal vascular precursors along a single developmental axis, producing arteriovenous malformations that link the retina, optic pathway and midbrain on one side. These high-flow lesions consist of direct arterial-to-venous connections without an intervening capillary bed, leading to dilated tortuous vessels. In the retina this produces a racemose angioma that may compromise vision, while intracranial arteriovenous malformations carry a risk of haemorrhage, seizures and progressive neurological deficit. Overlying facial cutaneous vascular naevi reflect involvement of the same regional vascular field.
additionalDifferentials: Retinal capillary haemangioblastoma of von Hippel-Lindau disease
additionalInvestigations: Dilated fundus examination and retinal imaging to characterise the arteriovenous malformation
MRI of the brain to detect intracranial arteriovenous malformations
MRA or catheter angiography to define the vascular anatomy
Ophthalmological assessment of visual acuity and fields
Neurological examination for cranial nerve and midbrain involvement
Fluorescein angiography of the retina where indicated
redFlags: Signs of intracranial haemorrhage such as sudden severe headache or acute neurological deficit
New seizures or progressive neurological signs
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the extent and location of the arteriovenous malformations; small stable lesions may remain asymptomatic, but large intracranial malformations carry a risk of haemorrhage and neurological morbidity, and extensive retinal involvement can cause permanent visual loss.
pitfalls: Treating a retinal arteriovenous malformation as isolated without neuroimaging for intracranial lesions
Overlooking a subtle facial vascular naevus that signals deeper malformation
Attempting intervention on high-flow lesions without full angiographic assessment
Confusing the retinal lesion with von Hippel-Lindau haemangioblastoma
